title: Red flags to look for when hiring an R&D tax credit advisor
description: Red flags when hiring an R&D tax credit advisor include no real §41 specialization, reconstructed documentation, boilerplate narratives and guarantees.
summary: US businesses hiring an R&D tax credit advisor should watch for red flags such as no genuine §41 specialization, routine work presented as qualified research, reconstructed documentation, boilerplate narratives, contingency fees and guaranteed outcomes. Choose an advisor whose claim will survive IRS examination, because the taxpayer signs the return and bears disallowance, interest and penalty risk.

body.text: US businesses hiring an R&D tax credit advisor should watch for red flags such as no genuine §41 specialization, routine work presented as qualified research, reconstructed documentation, boilerplate narratives, contingency fees and guaranteed outcomes. Choose an advisor whose claim will survive IRS examination, because the taxpayer signs the return and bears disallowance, interest and penalty risk.
This report is general information, not legal or tax advice, and readers should confirm how any rule applies to their own facts with a qualified tax professional.
1. Why the Choice of Advisor Carries Real Risk

The federal credit for increasing research activities is codified at Internal Revenue Code (IRC) §41. The taxpayer, not the advisor, signs the return and carries the burden of substantiating the credit, so an advisor's errors become the client's disallowance, interest and penalty exposure.
1.1 Heightened scrutiny (a UK data point)

HMRC estimated error and fraud in its R&D tax relief schemes at £469m for 2021–22, up from £336m in 2020–21, equal to an overall rate of 4.9%, as reported from the National Audit Office's audit of HMRC's 2021–22 accounts. This figure describes the UK regime only and should not be read as a measure of the US §41 credit. It is useful to a US reader only as an illustration of how quickly a tax authority tightens its review once aggressive claim marketing becomes widespread.

The reasons it lists are: the company lacked a "competent professional"; the work was treated as subcontracted; and the evidence of an advance or of technical uncertainties was insufficient. "Competent professional" and "advance" are terms of the UK regime, not of IRC §41. The US equivalents are the statutory elements in §41(d)(1), discussed under Red Flag 1. The same article says unscrupulous firms marketed "guaranteed" claims and "free money" to SMEs, and that this fed the rapid growth in claims.
1.2 The cost of a failed claim: disallowance and penalties

The IRS accuracy-related penalty under IRC §6662 is 20% of the portion of an underpayment attributable to, among other things, negligence or disregard of rules or regulations, or a substantial understatement of income tax. For corporations other than S corporations or personal holding companies, an understatement is substantial when it exceeds the lesser of 10% of the tax required to be shown on the return (or, if greater, $10,000) or $10,000,000.

Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (U.S. Tax Court, Docket No. 4759-22, filed December 23, 2024, Judge Greaves) shows that both risks are real. The taxpayer was a multidisciplinary engineering consulting firm that designs mechanical, electrical, plumbing and fire-protection systems. The court denied its research credits and sustained the IRS's accuracy-related penalties. One practitioner summary (Strike Tax) reports that the penalty was upheld under the parties' stipulation; this procedural detail comes from commentary, not the opinion text.

Analysis: for a prospective client, the lesson is that a disallowed credit is not a neutral outcome. The tax that the credit offset becomes due with interest, and a penalty may be added on top. An advisor who cannot explain how a claim will be defended against a §6662 penalty has not finished the job.
1.3 More disclosure at filing

Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities, was revised in December 2024 (IRS form revision "1224"). The IRS's About Form 6765 page lists the Instructions for Form 6765 as the December 2025 revision; the final instructions were released in early February 2026. The revised form added Section G, Business Component Information, alongside expanded disclosures in Sections E and F.

Section G was optional for tax year 2024. In IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025) the IRS made it optional for all filers for tax year 2025 (processing year 2026) as well. For tax year 2026 (processing year 2027) and later, Section G is mandatory, with optional reporting for two groups: (1) qualified small business taxpayers under IRC §41(h)(3) who check the box to claim the reduced payroll tax credit; and (2) taxpayers with total qualified research expenses of $1.5 million or less at the controlled group level and gross receipts of $50 million or less under §448(c)(3), who claim the credit on an original filed return. The final February 2026 instructions confirmed this timeline. For calendar-year taxpayers, that means returns filed in 2027 for the 2026 tax year are the first for which most filers must complete Section G.

For context on the first exception group, IRC §41(h)(3) generally treats a corporation or partnership as a qualified small business for a taxable year if its gross receipts for that year are less than $5,000,000 and it had no gross receipts for any taxable year before the five-taxable-year period ending with that year. The payroll tax election itself is made under §41(h)(1).

For research credit refund claims, News Release IR-2021-203 (October 2021) set out required elements for claims filed after January 10, 2022. According to The Tax Adviser (October 2025), in FAQ 21, updated June 18, 2024, the IRS dropped two elements at filing: the names of the individuals who performed each research activity, and the information each individual sought to discover. The IRS can still ask for both during an audit. Practitioner coverage of IR-2025-99 (Crowe) also reports that the IRS extended the transition period during which a taxpayer has 45 days to perfect a deficient research credit refund claim through January 10, 2027.

In Harper v. United States, No. 19-55933 (9th Cir. filed February 25, 2021), the court reversed the district court's dismissal (No. 3:18-cv-02110, S.D. Cal., April 25, 2019). It held that the IRS had waived the refund-claim specificity requirement by examining the research credit claims on the merits over several years. The memorandum is unpublished and is not precedent except as provided by Ninth Circuit Rule 36-3. Analysis: the case shows that the specificity requirement is litigated, but it is a taxpayer win on waiver. The trend toward documentation at filing rests on the Form 6765 changes and the refund-claim requirements above, and a careful advisor will not plan on the IRS waiving a defect the way it did in Harper.
2. Red Flags in Technical Expertise
Red Flag 1: No genuine R&D specialization

The legal test for eligibility is technical. Under IRC §41(d)(1), qualified research must (A) involve expenditures that are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under §174A (the cross-reference in the current statutory text); (B) be undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature and whose application is intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component of the taxpayer; and (C) be research of which substantially all of the activities are elements of a process of experimentation for a permitted purpose relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability or quality. Grantica's UK guidance lists the absence of the necessary credentials and track record as a red flag. The ICAEW's June 2020 PCRT guidance on R&D services says advisers with limited R&D experience should think carefully about how they describe their services.

Analysis: a firm's founding date or exclusive focus can be a useful signal, but neither proves competence. Ask who will run the technical interviews, what engineering or scientific background those people have, and how activities will be tested against each element of §41(d). An advisor who answers in terms of tax percentages rather than technical uncertainty and experimentation is describing a sales process, not a qualification review.
Red Flag 2: Routine work presented as qualified research

Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(6) treats the "substantially all" requirement as met only if 80% or more of the research activities for a business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, are elements of a process of experimentation. In Phoenix Design Group, practitioner analysis (KBKG) reports that the court found many of the firm's activities to be routine engineering rather than qualified research. It also reports that merely complying with building codes was not enough, and that the taxpayer did not show the substantially-all test was met. Activities that are only connected to a broader plan resembling the scientific method did not pass.

Analysis: an advisor who presents ordinary design, customization or code-compliance work as experimentation, without evidence that alternatives were systematically evaluated, is exposing the whole claim. Because the 80% test is applied business component by business component, a credible advisor will be able to show how each component was scoped and why its experimentation share clears the threshold. Section G's business-component reporting from tax year 2026 makes that analysis visible on the face of the return.
Red Flag 3: Overstated staff time and mishandled costs

The HMRC-focused Tax Adviser article identifies overstated staff apportionments, especially at 100%, as high risk. On the US side, IRC §41(b)(3)(A) generally counts contract research expenses at 65% of amounts paid or incurred to any person other than an employee of the taxpayer for qualified research; the statute raises that percentage to 75% for amounts paid to qualified research consortia and to 100% for certain energy research. K-38 Consulting, a consultancy source, notes two further risks: supply costs that lack a direct link to qualified research, and wage allocations based on guesswork.

Analysis: a reliable advisor builds wage qualified research expenses from traceable time and project data, applies the correct contract research percentage to contractors, and leaves out overhead. Be cautious of an advisor who assigns 100% of an employee's time to research without records, or who includes contractor payments at full value without explaining the statutory limit.
3. Red Flags in Methodology and Documentation
Red Flag 4: Documentation reconstructed after the fact

K-38 Consulting advises that records made while the work happens give the strongest audit protection. Taft's analysis of recent cases reads Phoenix Design Group as preferring documentation over testimony.

Analysis: be cautious of an advisor whose plan is to rebuild technical narratives from general ledgers months or years later. Prefer project plans, time records, test logs and version-controlled technical records created during the work. With Section G requiring business-component detail for most filers from tax year 2026, records captured during the year are also the practical way to meet the filing requirement, not only a defense in an audit.
Red Flag 5: Missing or boilerplate technical narratives

K-38 Consulting says a narrative should cover the technological advances sought, the obstacles faced, the resources used and the outcomes. In the UK context, the Tax Adviser article says documentation should leave the company "credible and comfortable when explaining to HMRC" how its projects qualify.

Analysis: a narrative written from a template, with the same wording repeated across projects, is a warning sign because it cannot show the project-specific uncertainty and experimentation that §41(d) requires. Ask to see a redacted sample narrative before signing.
Red Flag 6: No transparent process, or pressure to sign
Grantica lists three red flags here: a consultant who is not open about fees, process or expertise; one without a clear, well-defined plan; and one who pressures the client to sign quickly.

Analysis: a credible proposal names the data to be collected, the interviews, the method for mapping costs to business components, the deliverables, and who will support the client if the IRS opens an examination. Pressure to sign before that information is provided is itself a reason to slow down.
4. Red Flags in Ethical and Financial Practices
Red Flag 7: Fees that reward aggressive claims

ICAEW's PCRT guidance says members must follow the Fundamental Principles, serve clients while upholding the profession's reputation, and consider the wider public interest. It also bars misleading claims on websites, citing examples such as "100% of claims agreed."
The PCRT R&D guidance page reviewed (June 9, 2020) does not address contingent fees.

cells: Percentage of credit claimed or secured
Incentive to maximize the claim, raising examination and penalty exposure
Agreed price for a defined scope
Disputes over scope if records are poor or the work is complex
Time spent by the advisor's staff
Higher cost when client records need heavy reconstruction

body.text: Red Flag 8: Guaranteed outcomes and unrealistic promises

Grantica advises ending the conversation if a consultant talks about "free money." The ICAEW gives "HMRC approved methodology" as an example of a misleading claim. The blog describes bad actors who misled businesses under the guise of lawful services, often for large fees, and urges taxpayers to remember that if it sounds too good to be true, it probably is.

Analysis: nobody can guarantee a credit amount before reviewing the client's activities and records. A promise of an "IRS-approved" method has no basis, because the IRS does not pre-approve any advisor's methodology, and a quoted credit amount given before any technical review is a sign the number was built to sell the engagement.
5.1 Governance and fees

A prospective client should confirm in the engagement letter exactly how any fee is calculated, whether any part of it depends on the credit amount, and what happens to the fee if the credit is later reduced on examination.
ISO states that ISO 31000 provides guidelines and cannot be used for certification, and ISO lists the 2009 edition as withdrawn, replaced by ISO 31000:2018.
5.2 Documentation technology and review

The announcement describes real-time documentation capture of technical progress and qualifying activities as they occur, which builds a contemporaneous audit trail, along with AI-driven insights and a structured documentation framework.

Analysis: as Strike Tax's May 2026 commentary on Section G puts it, software can speed up documentation work but does not replace it. Whatever tool an advisor uses, ask who reviews its output and whether that reviewer has the technical background to judge the §41(d) elements.
5.3 Audit-defense coverage

TaxTrex's site describes creditARMOR as R&D tax credit insurance and an AI-driven risk-management platform that covers defense expenses, including CPA, tax attorney and specialist consultant fees. Analysis: covering defense costs is not the same as covering a disallowed credit, interest or penalties. Review the policy terms directly.
6. Due Diligence Checklist for Vetting an Advisor

items: Fee basis in writing. Ask whether any part of the fee depends on the credit amount.
Documentation method. Ask how records will be captured during the work rather than rebuilt at year-end (Red Flag 4).
Case-law awareness. Ask how the advisor screens out routine engineering and applies the 80% substantially-all rule, with reference to Phoenix Design Group (Red Flag 2).

Form 6765 readiness. Ask how the advisor will gather business-component data for Section G, which is mandatory from tax year 2026 for most filers, and whether your company falls within either exception (a qualified small business making the payroll election, or $1.5 million or less in QREs and $50 million or less in gross receipts on an original return).

Refund-claim requirements. If the engagement includes amended returns, ask how the advisor will meet the IRS's specificity requirements for research credit refund claims and handle the 45-day perfection period.
Audit support. Ask what examination support is included and, if insurance is offered, what it actually covers.
